utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Krsnik, are you ready for your witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. Yes, I'm ready, as always.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are there any protective measures for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Krsnik. Examined by Mr. Krsnik:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we start, let me say a few things to you. And to tell you that our conversation will, by and large, address only some of the more important topics in your analysis. Their Honours have read your report so that we shall not waste time. And I'd like to ask you, because I know that you are very proficient in English, please follow the transcript that is in front of you and when you see this dot stop, then find the best way, not too slow, not too fast and always wait for me to finish my question and then start answering it. I believe this is all that I can say by way of introduction and as we talk, if a problem arises I will give you a warning. So let's start. As always, most distinguished doctor, will you please briefly tell your -- something about your CV? Of course I mean your professional career. And, of course, your full name.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I am Mladen Ancic. I was born in 1955. I completed my primary, secondary education in Sarajevo, where I was born. I read and graduated from the -- from historical studies in Sarajevo at the faculty of philosophy in Sarajevo and then in 1985, I obtained my MA degree in Belgrade. Then worked at the Memorial Centre Vraca in Sarajevo, that -- at the Institute of History in Sarajevo. During the war, I left Sarajevo, moved to Zadar, and there I got a job with the Institute for History of the Croat -- Croatian Academy of Sciences and Arts. I obtained my Ph.D. in Zagreb in 1996. I teach at the Croatian Studies department of the University of Zagreb and I have the title of docent. I teach at the post-graduate studies of the faculty in Zagreb -- in Zadar. I've published five books, dozens of papers in scientific journals. Just a moment? May I go back? I'd like -- I'd rather that it says here "learned" rather than "scientific."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Every comment that you have is welcome, because the interpretation -- I mean to understand what you are saying in the spirit of the language so please do intervene whenever you think it is necessary.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: So I published dozens of papers in learned journals in Bosnia-Herzegovina in Croatia, in Austria, in England, and that would be my CV, briefly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you worked for the Vraca Memorial Park. Can you tell us what that is?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The Vraca Memorial Centre is practically the Holocaust museum in Sarajevo, the museum of the victims of the Holocaust in Sarajevo and I worked there for five years as an associate addressing the latest history of Bosnia-Herzegovina and at the same time studying -- doing research into what was my wish to do and that was the medieval history briefly. I addressed, I studied, I also wrote for the media, especially during the war. I was the editor of the educational programme of the Sarajevo Television. And I was -- and I was responsible -- I was the editor of history courses. So this would roughly be the things that define my professional career.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you have authored a number of books, and we have the titles in your CV. What I'd like to know is are you also the author of the book, "Who went wrong in Bosnia?"

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you, being its author, can you tell us what the book is about?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: That book is in point of fact a collection of texts which I published in periodicals in an attempt to explain where is the link between what is history and what is the political reality of the country I live in, and its neighbours. I also made recourse to what is my personal experience and the experience of my friends, acquaintances, people I communicate with. It was a strange procedure for a historian, strange, insofar as I also lived at a strange time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that book, I've noticed -- I mean preparing to meet you, I read an interesting detail. You described a meeting in Sarajevo with very interesting participants. Some of them appeared here as permanent expert witnesses for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was quite surprised when my friend and colleague, professor Dr. Ante Markotic, who has already been here incidentally, told me that he had taken part in a strange, in an odd dinner in Sarajevo in 1991, that dinner was organised by an official of the American embassy in Belgrade. He brought together several university professors and tried to learn from them something about their views of the then situation in Bosnia and Herzegovina. One of the participants was Professor Pajic who on that occasion said -- expressed a view that the situation in Bosnia-Herzegovina could be resolved if several heads were taken off. And that came to me as a shock, that a man with such views figured as an expert wherever.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: M'hm. Right. But we can come back to that later. I'd now like to ask you what was the assignment that the Defence gave you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: My assignment was to evaluate the finding of an expert witness for the Prosecution, Dr. Donia, to establish how much does it conform to the standards governing the work of historians, how much does it conform to the general knowledge of the history of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and finally to write a study, to write a treatise as to how, in what way, history defines the causes of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina and how it defines the patterns of behaviour of the participants to that war.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it your task to - since you're a historian - to help the Court with your expert testimony, to show that what happened in Bosnia did not happen out of the blue, wasn't parachuted down, as some claim?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I hope that the text which I submitted to this honourable Court and my verbal presentation will help towards the comprehension of the context of that conflict. But I need to round off my thought, for a historian the context is by far the most important word.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Follow the transcript. Follow the transcript. Now that you've touched upon this, will you tell the honourable Court which is the most important part of the work of a historian? What is a historian, basically?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: A man who engages in the reconstruction of what took place, a man who tries to identify individual events, establish how they came to pass, and then the most important part. From those individual events, one needs to put together a net, which explains the whole historical movement, the historical movement as a whole, the historical context as a whole or rather a social context as a whole which has vanished, which has vanished without retrieve and which only we the historians know how to reconstruct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: My next logical question, did Dr. Donia as the expert witness for the Prosecution apply such an approach when he prepared his reports and testimonies before this Court?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Before I answer that question, I will have to ask you for some time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, of course. I understand that you cannot answer yes or no, but let us not spend too much time and let us also try to be interesting.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I come from an academic community in which there is no simple answer to any question. Therefore, the meeting with Dr. Donia, not personal but through texts because I've never met Dr. Donia, represented a strange experience for me. I discovered a historian with two faces. One face is the face outlined by his dissertation and a very serious book emerged from it, titled, "Under the double eagle." The second face is the one revealed by texts in a book called "Bosnia - tradition betrayed," and the findings which Dr. Donia presented to this honourable Court. One face is the face of a serious historian, who worked on many documents, who consulted very relevant literature and managed to create an interesting, valuable book.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. When was this book written, which year?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It was published in 1978.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since 1978, has he appeared in the literature related to history?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Bibliography, in periodicals, his name never appeared after that, until the mid-1990s. Dr. Donia spent that time working for the Merrill Lynch Investment Fund. It is a fact that for an entire decade, if not even longer, he was not in the academic community. He did not read new literature on a day-to-day basis and that is mirrored in this other face. This other face reveals a historian who uses only secondary sources, secondary sources that are based in their own right on secondary sources yet again. For a historian, the key thing is to be in a constant contact with documents that pertain to the time that he is dealing with. I have carefully looked at the authorities upon which Dr. Donia relies, and indeed, I could bore you to tears here by various quotations that would show and prove what I have just said. The trouble that stems from this, though, and that fully shows the problems that Dr. Donia encounters can be illustrated by one example, if you allow me to quote it, namely at one point in time, Dr. Donia invokes the memoirs of Lord Owen. However, he does not draw anything out of these memoirs that would be a fact. From these memoirs he draws a judgement, rather Lord Owen's judgement, concerning Dr. Franjo Tudjman, at that time the President of the Republic of Croatia. For a conscientious and serious historian, that is an impermissible thing. By your leave, just one more sentence. Lord Owen's judgement concerning another person, actually says a lot about Lord Owen himself, and very little about the man that this judgement pertains to. The mistake that the expert makes in such a way, and that is not his only mistake, brings him into waters that can no longer be considered serious scholarly effort. Of course, other mistakes are derived from that as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us proceed in a logical sequence. So let me ask you the following: Do you agree with Dr. Donia's assertion that mediaeval times in Bosnia-Herzegovina were characterised by a clash between Catholicism and Orthodoxy, that is to say in the territory that we call Bosnia nowadays, of course you will better versed in these matters so could you say something about this?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Indeed. Dr. Donia has a problem already with the notion of Bosnia-Herzegovina in historical dimensions. What this notion means from a geographical point of view, at different points in time, when it appears, who uses it and for what reasons. However, we can go back to that a bit later. The basic thesis in this case is actually something that has nothing to do with the reality of mediaeval Bosnia. Documents, archaeology, all of this together shows that in the area that we call mediaeval Bosnia, all the way up to the end of the 14th century, there is not a single Orthodox Church. Therefore, it is unclear how this period of time could be marked at all by a clash between Catholicism and Orthodoxy. Of course, I cannot claim, nor do I know, whether this is a mistake that stems from ignorance, indolence or intention. However, some things that Dr. Donia wrote and said can be spelled out in a bit more specific terms therefore. For example, Dr. Donia uses, as a source, various censuses of Bosnia-Herzegovina, from 1910 and 1981, and he compares the numerical ratios in terms of the members of various ethnic communities at these points in time. However, the trouble is that the geographical notions that he uses do not have the same meaning in 1910 and in 1981.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Explain that.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: For example, the notion of Fojnica, in the 1910 census corresponds to the notions of Fojnica, Kiseljak and Busovaca in 1981 because the administrative setup of that area is different. The notion of Travnik from the 1910 census corresponds to the notions of Travnik, Novi Travnik and Vitez from the 1981 census. A serious historian would take note of such things, take them into consideration, or at least show that he knows about this. That is the type of mistake that can be considered a consequence of possible indolence or possible ignorance. Another type of mistake or ignorance, formal ignorance, is the following example. Dr. Donia claims that he does not know how big a part of Croatia was under the control of the rebel forces of the Serbs from Croatia in 1992. This is certainly a very relevant matter for understanding the context of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Furthermore, can it be claimed that it was only the Catholics who fought for religious, educational and cultural autonomy under the Ottoman rule? Actually, the question is as follows: Are there significant, meaningful differences between the Orthodox, the Muslims and the Catholics under Ottoman rule?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Indeed so. Indeed, there are. And these differences are a key point that is conducive to understanding the continuity which finally leads to the conflict in 1992. All three religious communities become the key of the socialness of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina, or rather the area that we call Bosnia-Herzegovina nowadays. Please, I would like this word "socialness" to be interpreted as "social consciousness," because that would more clearly reflect what I actually meant. I am referring to an awareness as to where a person belongs in that society. Belonging to a religious community in that society marks a person in terms of how he will make a distinction between "we" and "us" in the world. The pattern created at that point in time is going to pressure and does pressure the consciousness of the inhabitants of Bosnia-Herzegovina, until the present day, as a historical burden which one cannot get rid of even if one wishes to do so. The conclusion is that the differences that are caused by religious affiliation in the Ottoman Empire, thanks to the fact that the Ottoman Empire was the way it was, it was what we could nowadays call a religious state. All of that led to the following: Religious affiliation became the key to one's awareness, consciousness, as to where a person belonged to in that society.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It would be logical, of course, to ask you now, I think that we have now come to the question of nationality. According to your findings, this history starts in the medieval times, not only in the 19th century, not as late as the 19th century and this comes as a counterbalance to Yugoslavness. Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: What really surprised me in Dr. Donia's findings was the fact that he, when debating the problem of nations in Bosnia-Herzegovina, did not seek to rely on the rich body of modern literature that pertains to this question. That surprised me even more because Dr. Donia, in his dissertation, relied upon and used extensively the results of social anthropology. In the findings that he presented to this honourable Trial Chamber, had he repeated that procedure, and had he relied upon, at least in part, the vast literature that speaks about the roots of modern nationalism -- I'm using the word "nationalism" here in the scientific meaning of the word, as this term is used to describe the process of creating modern nations. So had Dr. Donia used at least part of that literature, then the honourable Trial Chamber would have got a completely different picture about this, different to the extent to which the role of ethnic communities would have been more pronounced, those that have been in existence since the medieval times, and that actually are the cradle of modern nations. In this way, the vast array of issues that has to deal with the problem of nations would have looked completely differently.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Very briefly, if you could just give me a brief answer too, which sources did Dr. Donia use and where is this rich literature and rich documentation that he did not use and that he should have used, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The literature is certainly far more accessible to Dr. Donia than to me. Libraries and resources that are available to persons dealing with this subject matter where Dr. Donia lives are incomparably better organised and more accessible than in the environment in which I live, on the one hand. On the other hand, documents are a major problem, a major problem, because as concerns the events of the past 30 years, most of them are not accessible. That is one of the things that Dr. Donia actually had to be aware of. Actually his dissertation reveals how a political movement came into being, but he reveals that to a large extent due to the availability of documents that are of a secret nature, that is to say police reports, findings of intelligence services from the end of the 19th century; in a word, a type of documents that nowadays are not nearly as accessible to us now as the documents pertaining to the 19th century are. This distance that is opened up over the years can show very unusual results. For example, modern historians look at what Austro-Hungarian policies in Bosnia-Herzegovina were like after Austro-Hungary occupied this country. Very unusual things were discovered. We have a problem with the previous sentence actually.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That's why I'm asking to you look at the transcript. I am not always fortunate enough in having a witness whose English is very good so I really want to you follow the transcript all the time, because of the dynamics of your speech, but also I want to you check whether everything is in the spirit of the language that you have been using.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I said something different here. I said that modern historians, when they look at the policy of Austro-Hungary in Bosnia-Herzegovina, revealed something unusual, something that the contemporaries could not have known. The man who governed Bosnia-Herzegovina for 20 years on behalf of Austro-Hungary, and his name was Benjamin Kallay, tried, in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- and at that time there were already three ethnic communities that were on the road of the creation of a modern nation -- he tried to create out of them a single political body. His intimate writings revealed, however, that the objective of such efforts was to de-Islamise the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina. That is one such case. Subsequent insight makes it possible to create a more reliable picture, and such procedures are recommended, especially in situations where a great deal remains unclear.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us then move to the most logical question. As a historian, can you tell us when does the Bosniak nation come into being?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: European historians and theoreticians too, of what we call the national problem -- here theoreticians is missing. People who engage in the theory of ethnic relations, the translation is --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're quite free to correct it.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: So those people are today interested in Bosnia and Herzegovina and accord a great deal of attention to Bosnia-Herzegovina, because they can follow how a modern nation is coming into being today. Why is that interesting? Modern European nations came into being in the 19th century, and as of the 19th century, there has been no cases of emergence of new nations in Europe. However, it is precisely in Bosnia-Herzegovina, over the past ten or 15 years, that a modern nation began to emerge. Members of that community acquire awareness of their belonging to a community and that awareness is politically highly relevant. And that is what attracts the attention of many authors in Europe and the world over. So that at present, we can follow what we only knew from hearsay about the 19th century, namely in the process of building a modern nation, and tradition are of extraordinary importance and English historian Eric Hobsbawm in a collection which he edited himself, showed how, in the 19th century, traditions were invented to help towards the integration of a modern nation. Today, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, we can follow such a historiographic production on a large scale. It, that is this historiography, engages in creating a myth about history and the past, which is -- which ought to prove the deep roots of the modern nation. That historiography has been assessed in this way even by Dr. Donia in one of his recent works. In a text which, in the scientific classification, is called a survey, review, Dr. Donia presents several latest works published in Sarajevo, historical books. He concludes -- in his review he concludes that these works are demonstrating how a Bosniak -- how Bosniak historians would like their history to look like, rather than what it truly looks like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I interrupt while we are at it? From what I understand from what you're saying you've been asked several questions, none of which you've given an answer to but what you've said is interesting. Is what you're saying is that you oppose Dr. Donia's theory that there is such a thing as a separate Bosnian Bosniak identity, that in other words it isn't just religious differences according to Dr. Donia, and according to you, it's a reinvented history or a totally invented history to find a separate identity. Are you saying that they are not any different, that the Muslim nation or ethnic group is not the descendant of a separate group, that they are people who changed their religion and are now busily inventing a past? That seems to be what I understand so we can know exactly what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, that is not what I'm trying to say. I am trying to say that the old religious identity under the modernising influences, some were faster, some were slower, grows into a modern identity, social identity, which we term "nation" at present. That in the Bosniak case, this process, for a variety of reasons, is late.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: That's very unclear to me. Are you disagreeing with Dr. Donia or are you agreeing with him up to a point? It's not clear to me what you're saying. You were asked about ten minutes ago when did the Bosniak nation come into being, and my understanding from your paper is that the word "Bosniak" was first used by this governor from Austro -- Austria-Hungary and that he invented that word and the effect of the word was the de-Islamisation of that group of people. But that doesn't -- that's got nothing to do with the question Mr. Krsnik asked. Mr. Krsnik asked when did the Bosniak nation come into being? Well, surely the question is before you gave it the name Bosniak, did the group exist as a separate entity or ethnic group even before the concept of nationhood? That I think is what Mr. Krsnik was asking you and I'm very interested in the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My -- in my answer, I start from the fact that terms have a history of their own, that at different times different notions are used in different ways, that at one and the same time, different people use them with different purposes in mind. Benjamin Kallay endeavoured to use the term "Bosniak" for his own purpose. Present-day -- the present-day political elite endeavours to use this same notion for their own -- for its own purposes. And having said that, I must emphasise that in conformity with the modern interpretation, a nation is exclusively a form of massive political mobilisation, that as a manner of massive political mobilisation, it relies -- it looks for support in what it has found in the society, that is, its actors look for support in the things they've found in a society, and in this particular case, it means ethnic identities. In the 19th century and for the most part of the 20th century, the Bosniak nation, as we call it today, did not have support in the old name of the ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Professor, will you please try to speak in a language which is comprehensible to us who are laymen? Try to explain simply when did the Bosniak nation come into being, as we call it today, and of course, if you cannot do that in a nutshell, please then try to make some of the notions more comprehensible to us who are lay, because you are really beyond comprehension.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Very well, it's like this. I think that the whole picture will become easy to understand the moment I say that in Sarajevo, as the capital of Bosnia and Herzegovina, you do not have a single monument to any historical -- of any historical figure from the national past. In Zagreb, for comparison's sake, what does that mean? In Zagreb, as you come out of the railway station, you come across the monument of King Tomislav. All the inhabitants of Croatia, when they arrive in Zagreb, acquire awareness of their common past when they cast a look at the monument. He is their old king. In Belgrade likewise. In every city in western Europe, again likewise. In Sarajevo, the first king of the mediaeval Bosnia had a street, that is, a street named after him, and it was a side street. Is the picture clear now?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To me, of course it is, but I want you to explain it to the honourable Court and you still have not answered to me in a comprehensible language, when does the Bosniak nation come into being? I understand you, that you are saying that it is coming into being today, and that we are witnesses to its emergence but now the time is coming for a break. If you can do it now, then let us do it before the break. If not, then I will ask Their Honours to have the break and then we will come back to it because the crucial question that is of concern to us we want to you bring closer to us laymen of course if you can answer it, when did the Bosniak nation come into being, 1915, 1980 it began to evolve, you understand that is what I want to you to do, to bring it closer to us who are lay?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Right. So a nation in the modern sense comes into being at -- when people start to identify themselves by a name, a common name. In the case of the Bosniak nation, that moment could be situated in 1974. That name, as the name of people who are aware of the fact that they are Bosniaks, and that term is not used before that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters correction 1994, not 1974.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Since 1971, there is officially the name for members of that same community, and that is Muslims. Prior to 1971, members of that same community defined themselves by the fact that they were neither Serbs nor Muslims -- sorry, neither Croats. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Can I ask you this? Is it the situation that there was never in modern times, and I would say from the mid-19th century, never a time when the citizens of what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina called themselves Bosnians? Because when you go to the United Kingdom or Ireland, Bosnians mean Bosnian Muslims. If somebody says they are a Bosnian, everybody knows what they mean. That's why we use the term a Bosnian Serb and a Bosnian Croat. That means that they are people from Bosnia who are Orthodox and claim allegiance to Serbia and likewise Croatia but they are natives of what is now Bosnia-Herzegovina. So did Muslims never, if they were asked in the 19th century, if they were travelling in Europe, "what is your nationality?" Say, "We are Bosnians"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you now understand how things ought to be explained?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The name "Bosnian" Bosanac, in contrast with "Bosniak," Bosnjak -- [In English] The name Bosnian as contrast with the Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I understand that but the question I asked you, Professor Ancic, was, did these people before anyone invented the name Bosniak, not have an identity? The Ottomans were gone, the Austro-Hungarians were there, I mean these people were neither Arabs, Turks or Austro-Hungarians. They had an ethnic identity. Did they not describe themselves as Bosnians? After all, they came from Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They called themselves Bosnians, but Serbs and Croats also called themselves Bosnians because that is the definition, that is a definition, like, for instance, a Toscanian or a Lombard or Lombardian or for somebody who was born in Normandy in France. So it is a regional definition which does not imply political loyalty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, but they had a name. They were happy to stand up and say, "I'm a Bosnian." In the 19th century, the 18th century, before nationhood apart from very few countries had become fully established or maybe a century earlier, people were still saying that they were from smaller principalities of Italy or Germany. They might have said that they were English or French but they were much more likely I think as a historian, you would know, to say I'm a Norman, I'm a Provencal, I'm whatever, from the particular provinces. It was important so there was an identity which was Bosnian. So in that sense you don't disagree with Dr. Donia so far. What you're talking about is, I understand it, a suppression of an identity and a reemergence of something different. And we've had people here who spoke about a Muslim identity being suppressed or their religion or whatever, and Muslims always being unrecognised. And I think that's what -- we are going round and round in circles. If we are going to use Bosniak as opposed to Bosnian, to be the genesis of a new nation, that when somebody rechristens you or renames you suddenly you emerge for the first time and that's, I think, simply not so, but I don't know where this argument is getting us any way. Why are we getting bogged down? This is not what this expert came to talk about because you don't really deal with that in your paper to any great extent. The paper is not a criticism of Dr. Donia. I thought it was your view of the war and its motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall most certainly come to that, Your Honour, but you now prompt me, and experience in this courtroom for the past year, to try to explain how things are, because it is not how you understood it, Your Honour, because Bosnian and Bosniak is not the same in the present meaning of the modern nation, and that is why we brought this professor to explain it because I'm saying that the Bosnian nation did not -- never existed before 1994. We can speak about an ethnic community. We can speak about a religious community but not about a nation. And that is a major difference. And for the past year we have been listening here, myths and for the past year we have been listening what historians of the same a category, through Bosniak historiography try to market in the world and in this Tribunal through the Prosecutor's Office and that is why we have brought a historian -- of course I won't say that because it wouldn't be decent -- who he is considered one of the great men who know most about the Bosnian and Bosnian history. But it is time for the break so I will ask only a very short question to round off this topic because you know in the indictment we have the language and history and nation, so unless we analyse these terms and unless a historian explains them to us, then we shall leave here with wrong ideas because a court may not try history. History is facts and notorious facts. And this is my feeling is what is looked for here, that these judgements, pass judgement on history, especially with regard to the nation in its final stages, in the final stages of its taking shape.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. You want to answer that question? Yes, you may.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] An important fact, which is related to your question, is that your view of Bosnia is significantly different from the view of those who live in it. For those people, the marker is membership in a community and that community's name, who says of himself that he's a Bosnian says that he was born in Bosnia, and the one who says of himself that he's a Bosniak says of himself that he belongs to a modern nation, and these are highly relevant differences for those people, and because of these differences, they are up to going to war about them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, we have spent over an hour talking about those terminologies. As you rightly put it, we are not trying history. Of course, I believe that history is related to this case but what we want to hear is those facts in history which relate to what happened in 1992 and 1993. Now we have an expert witness and you will be allowed to ask some leading questions because we already have his statement at our hands and I hope during the break you could organise your questions and ask some direct questions which appear in his statement and which is related to what happened in 1992 and 1993. We will resume at 20 minutes past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was thinking during the break how to phrase my question in order to round off this topic, because I believe I realised what is the gist of our misunderstanding. So let me ask you like this. The Islamic religious community, that particular group, which peoples comprise it and when did this Islamic religious community begin to develop into a nation? Is that clear?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. The question is quite clear. The answer, as usual, is not simple.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please try to simplify it, and explain it to us in a comprehensible language?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I shall do my utmost to make it comprehensible even though it will certainly not be simple. So research and in this regard, we fortunately can rely on an author whose results so far have not been undermined, and that is the German historian who originally came from Bosnia-Herzegovina, and whose name is Srecko Dzaja. It is beyond any reasonable doubt that he established -- no. It is -- he established beyond any reasonable doubt, it is not beyond reasonable doubt that he established. He established beyond any reasonable doubt that the roots of the ethnic community from which the Bosniak nation would emerge are very diverse and they comprise descendants of the population which happened to be there at the time when the Ottomans conquered the territory, who embraced Islam, then parts of the population whom the sultan moved to that territory, be it of Turkish or some other origin, that is ready-made Muslims who were then sent to those areas. The third layer is a large number of refugees who headed for Bosnia and Herzegovina after the Ottoman empire lost a territory which we call today the Republic of Hungary, the Republic of Croatia, and even parts of the Republic of Slovakia. Therefore, at least three very important strata of different ethnic origin. First, under the influence of the Ottoman authority, these strata were put together in one group, which was originally defined only by their religious affiliation. Is that sufficiently short and clear?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I hope so. I am clear. I understand. But I'm not the one who is important here. But I believe that the Prosecutor will have some questions about it so we shall leave it to him and we shall move on. Can you tell the honourable Court if the Bosnian case, let me call it that, is singular or what one could call the Bosniak mosaic -- is that a situation specific of only this region, only the area that we today denote as Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The composition of the Bosnian society is specific, no doubt, but the type of relations which governed the society is not specific. A similar group of problems, a similar type of problems concerning the relations among different groups exists in other parts of Europe too. Understanding of such a type of relations which can be gained by an insight Into a situation in countries such as Northern Ireland, Wales and Denmark, and I picked out the example from a part of the English, from a work by an English anthropologist, Richard Jenkins show how this type of relations took shape in the course of history and how history determined how these problems would be solved. For instance, the history is the one which defines the model of the violent solution of problems in Northern Ireland, just as history is the one which defines the fact that similar problems in Wales are not solved by force. And at long last, history is the one which has brought about the fact that the Danish nationalism had no need for -- had no need to resort to this model of behaviour because of the different circumstances under which the modern-day Denmark emerged. All these examples show that, with all the specificities notwithstanding, Bosnia-Herzegovina is not an exception. But they also help to understand the problems of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, doctor, let's move on to modern history. Let us move to the events of the past ten years. By way of introduction, perhaps I would like to ask you, relying upon what you've just said about Europe, that is to say western Europe and central Europe, there have been multi-ethnic communities that have ethnic problems but these problems were not resolved in a drastic manner. Was there a possibility of resolving interethnic problems in Bosnia, those that were in latent conflict? Could they have been resolved without resorting to war? Can you address that by way of an introduction to this part of modern history? I would like to hear your thinking.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: You mean did history mean that problems would have to be resolved via -- by violence? This is not exactly predetermined, but tradition is the one that influenced the choice made by people who live in that area. Now, how did that happen? The traditional way of resolving such problems was, to a large extent, violence. Another important thing that affected these developments that led to a violent resolving of problems was the very beginning of the conflict. The role that at this beginning was played by that side which had an advantage to begin with, and which imposed violence as a method of resolving the problems. However, it is important to remember another important thing. The book of Istvan Bibo, a Hungarian historian, "The misery of small European nations," written in 1946, reads nowadays, as the scenario of the war in the former Yugoslavia. However, it was written at a time when it seemed to the author that Yugoslavia was the only country of central and eastern Europe that had resolved these problems. Bibo deals with the Czech Republic, Slovakia, Hungary, Romania and their mutual relations. However when these names are replaced by Serbs, Croats, Bosniaks, Slovenians and Macedonians, one actually obtains that which was Yugoslavia's reality after 1990. Once again, situations in the neighbourhood of Bosnia-Herzegovina, that is to say in the most immediate neighbourhood, are quite helpful in terms of understanding its own problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A subquestion: In its history, did Bosnia-Herzegovina ever have institutions, traditional state institutions, in which it would train, if I can put it that way, for the peaceful settlement of disputes? Have I been clear?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. First of all, a representative body where social conflicts of this type could have been resolved, the first one of this kind, was created in 1910, and it operated until the outbreak of the First World War in 1914. The second time that Bosnia-Herzegovina got any form of political representation within the boundaries of Bosnia-Herzegovina was in 1945. However, the body that was established then as the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina was actually just a mere transmitter for the government of the then-Communist Party. In it, there were no possibilities for resolving such problems. So when, in 1990, for the first time it was democratically elected, the population that entered the Assembly of Bosnia-Herzegovina never had any kind of experience with working in such a body. Never before that did Bosnia-Herzegovina have a true representative parliamentary body, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So we've come to 1990. Could you give us a brief summary, in terms of this historical distance of ten to 12 years? So let us restrict ourselves to Bosnia-Herzegovina. Let us view the true causes that led to the war.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: In response to such a question, I have to say straight away that the inaccessibility of a large number of documents makes it impossible to carry out a detailed analysis. However, since historians have to deal with the past even when there is not enough documents, from the present-day point of view, and on the basis of what is accessible today, a general framework can be portrayed within which the conflict broke out. This general framework would be the following: An attempt by the political establishment located in Belgrade to carry through a plan which can be called "internal secession." This notion was introduced in literature by a professor of political science from the Central European University in Budapest, Daniella Conversini. The point is that the Belgrade political establishment intended to take over parts of the former Yugoslavia and to create a new state out of them. In the attainment of this objective, that establishment did not refrain from the use of force either, which gave rise to the conflict. According to the possibilities we have available today in order to learn about these matters, this was actually the beginning of the war. However, due to different objectives, different political objectives, in the political elites within Bosnia-Herzegovina, for a while there was a concerted resistance to these endeavours made from Belgrade. Then the differences became too big. Therefore, they could no longer be concealed, these differences in political objectives, that is. They are what actually brought about a conflict within the conflict, and in this way, the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina got the form of a civil war. That would be the general framework that can be outlined on the basis of everything that is accessible nowadays.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In part you've already answered my question, because I had intended to ask you whether there were any differences between the protagonists of what was going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. Perhaps you've already answered this question in part already.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: There were major differences. These differences stem, first and foremost, from the initial positions. The Belgrade political establishment managed to have full control over a large part of the structures of the former Yugoslavia, that is to say the state authorities, the army, the police, the intelligence services, the diplomatic service. They put them all under their own control and used them for attaining their own objectives. On the other hand, neither the Croats nor the Muslims had any support in what could be described as the state apparatus. These two communities represented political elites -- were represented by political elites -- were represented by political elites that practically only in 1990 came to power, that did not have any experience in terms of governing a state, did not have experience with dealing with the structure of institutions that are called a government, and very soon these institutions fell apart anyway. So this is a major difference, and it stems from their very initial points of departure, initial positions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Precisely. This was your last sentence and I would like to you clarify that to the Trial Chamber. Does that mean that in 1992, the organised state apparatus, although the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina was internationally recognised, that this state apparatus did not really exist? There wasn't one?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: We have to proceed from the following, that according to a modern concept, a state is an institution which has a monopoly over force in a certain area, and which ensures for its subjects the meeting of a variety of social needs. At the point in time when Bosnia-Herzegovina was recognised as a state, the authorities that represented that state were no longer in a position to exercise a monopoly over the use of force, even in Sarajevo, their very own capital. At that moment, there were situations that showed that the authorities do not have any control over persons who had weapons in their hands. Another problem that these authorities had was the fact that already in the month of April, all -- about 80 to 90 per cent of all Serbs who were employed there had left state authorities and agencies. So these authorities could no longer carry out the functions that they were supposed to carry out. They did not have skilled persons who knew their jobs. A third problem for the authorities concerned was the fact that it was gradually losing formal legality too, and electoral legitimacy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you please clarify this last point?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It is simplest to explain it using the example of a body that is called the Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. The Presidency was a body that was inherited from the time of socialism. It was conceived as a body that would represent the entirety of the population of Bosnia-Herzegovina. It consisted of two representatives respectively of every one of the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and a 7th representative who was elected from the list of persons who felt themselves to be Yugoslavs and members of other ethnic communities. That is to say apart from the three ethnic communities mentioned. Until the month of June 1992, this Presidency remained without three of its elected members. The seventh member, who was elected from the list of those who did not belong to the three constituent peoples, started publicly and officially introducing himself as a member of one of these three ethnic communities, as a Muslim, that is, so at that time there weren't any Bosniaks yet. So this was the seventh member of that body who was supposed to represent persons who were neither Serbs nor Croats nor Muslims, and during the elections themselves, he declared himself as being one of those who declared themselves as Yugoslavs, so he betrayed the votes that he had won and he became a Muslim himself. So in that way, this body lost its lawful legality because it did not function in its entirety. It also lost its electoral legitimacy because it no longer represented the voters who had voted for it. In addition to that, and this is one of the unusual ideas that prevailed in the times of socialism, not a single member had any kind of supremacy in that body. All of them bore the same responsibility and all of them enjoyed the same rights. Chairing sessions was the right enjoyed by one of the members of that body, and this right was exercised in the following way. That member of the Presidency chaired sessions during one year. Then he would be replaced by another member of the Presidency who belonged to a different people. And then during the third year, a third member of the Presidency would chair sessions, a member coming from the third ethnic group. And during the fourth year of the four-year term of this body, these three Blank pages inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Pages 15755 to 15764. would take four-month turns. That was the legal procedure involved, or rather the procedure stipulated by law. However, this procedure could no longer be observed and there was no wish to have it observed, so the man who happened to be at the head of that body gave himself the right to permanently chair that body. As a matter of fact, he even allowed himself, in colloquial speech, to use the title "president". These were certainly problems that require very careful explanations, detailed explanations, too, because such acts can cause major confusion among persons who are not well-versed in the reality of the world from which the protagonists hail. When somebody introduces himself as the president, and when he introduces himself as such worldwide, then this comes across as something that people worldwide perceive as a president, then a person who is elected to such a position, who has a full mandate to reach decisions and who is responsible for his actions. However, in this particular case, it was not so, not even according to law. So the notion that is were being used did not correspond to the reality of the world from which they came. I don't know if I've been clear enough on this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Absolutely so, because for a year now, we've been listening to attempts made by the office of the Prosecution of course to portray the President of the Presidency that way, the way you've just explained it. Of course you are the person who is supposed to say the name of this man?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes, the man [Realtime transcript read in error "plan"] who chaired the Presidency at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It's supposed to read "the man" not "the plan" who chaired. The man who chaired the Presidency was Alija Izetbegovic. May I just add one more thing? Something that will shed more light on the situation involved? In Bosnia-Herzegovina itself, there were three men who were called president. They had the same legitimate right to that title. Because none of them had an electorate behind him whose president he would be. So all of them, in a way, were self-proclaimed presidents.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know about the situation concerning the constitutional court sometime in November, 1992, because here in this courtroom, attempts are being made to portray it as a constitutional, legal body that actually functioned.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The other agencies of state authority, none of them operated in full strength, and the same is true of the constitutional court. True, I am not an expert who can authoritatively speak about those problems, but I can affirm with certainty that the system of state authority fell, indeed, apart in 1992, and I do not know why would the constitutional court be an exception.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, please, to cut a long story short because I want to hand you over to the gentleman in the Prosecution as soon as possible, apart from all the circumstances in -- concerning the emergence of the HZ HB, what I would like you to explain to the Court is whether the HZ HB, that is the HR HB, ever applied for international recognition as a state. And I will have two side questions to that. So first did it ever request to be recognised? And will you explain the Court too whether the international community either in the Washington or in Dayton Accords recognised all its laws which are still in force and in use? And the Washington Agreement also envisaged a confederation between the federation of the Bosniaks and Muslims, and the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, subsequently the Croat Republic of Herceg-Bosna, could not apply for the international recognition because it emerged as an ad hoc body which was to fill in the political void after the disintegration of the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I do not know how could it apply for international recognition if, in all the documents, it said the name of Bosnia and Herzegovina. That much about the international recognition. The category of international recognition obviously was not a matter that was on the agenda for Herceg-Bosna, whether we speak about the community or the republic, subsequent republic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what about the laws and the confederation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The Washington Agreement recognised the de facto situation, that is, subsequently legitimization of the Croat community and Croat Republic Herceg-Bosna by the fact that its laws were recognised. The Dayton Accords, however, is something completely different. The Dayton Accords subsequently, in retrospection, in retrospect, recognised that a state called the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, in point of fact never worked. The Dayton Accords drew the political landscape of Bosnia-Herzegovina as if the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina has never existed. The Dayton Accords put in place Bosnia and Herzegovina, and even eliminated the name Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, the name under which this -- that country was recognised in 1992, as a composite state, which the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina was not. And the Dayton Accords revised the provisions of the Washington Agreement if they ran counter to what was achieved in Dayton.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So, please, from Dayton until today, what does it look like, and its real name is the state of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What does it look like? And is there a government of the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina? Who represents that state, Bosnia and Herzegovina? Please explain to the Court, as briefly as possible, from Dayton to this day.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Here we have problems with the translation of individual terms, because translated terms can always cause a confusion. So please tell me what you meant -- what you had in mind, because there is a body which is called the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. If that is what you meant, then such a body does not exist. In Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is a body called the council of ministers, and having said that, the Dayton Accords and the constitution of Bosnia-Herzegovina avoid explicitly the term "government." That is, "vlada". The term "government" is used explicitly to denote bodies in two constituent states of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So there is the government of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there is the government of the Republika Srpska, but there are ten more governments in every county, cantons that make up the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina. So with your permission, to put this matter on a level at which the inhabitants of Bosnia and Herzegovina come across every day, in the daily use, in the media in Bosnia-Herzegovina, the term "government", "vlada", of Bosnia-Herzegovina is never used but only and exclusively the term "the council of ministers." To go into reasons why that is so, the reasons for the situation would take us too far.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, please. This is a very important topic and will you please explain to the Court these two states within one state? So the Federation of the Bosniaks and Muslims, and the Republika Srpska. Which are their powers and what powers have they transferred to the joint state? Which, since the Dayton has been called the state of Bosnia and Herzegovina, to clarify this, because you know for the past year, I've been listening in this courtroom, that is the whole world has been listening, to the Prosecutor who keeps saying, this document was given me by the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina and secondly, he is setting out to say that there is such a thing as the government of Bosnia-Herzegovina. You know, these are important issues. So let us see --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I was trying to avoid interrupting counsel but the time has come for a couple of things. Again I object to the attacks on the politics of counsel, if that's an issue. Number one. The Chamber has heard that before. Number 2, I had the firm understanding, perhaps the Chamber did as well, that this was an expert on mediaeval Yugoslavian history and it seems to me we have gone very far afield from mediaeval Yugoslav history to what we are talking about now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, as you know, Mr. Scott, that this Trial Chamber allowed this witness to testify on certain issues which is related to 1992 and 1993, on the conflict which is the subject matter of this case. And the matter of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina has been raised many, many times during the proceedings. This witness is the last witness in the Defence case, and he is an expert witness. Taking all those factors into consideration, we will allow this witness to answer that question from his perspective. Of course the Prosecution has plenty of opportunity to challenge whatever this witness says. Witness, you may answer the question, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not consider myself an expert on the constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but whilst involved in my job, I read documents of relevance to your questions, and I can reproduce their contents to the extent that will satisfy what you're after. The council of ministers in Bosnia and Herzegovina has the mandate over the foreign policy, foreign affairs, foreign trade, including customs, communications of importance for the entire Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has powers to control the borders of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It has powers involved in the return of people to the entities from which they had been expelled, from which they have been expelled, and that would be more or less it. On the other hand, all the other powers, all the other jurisdiction concerning state administration and state bodies, belong to what the Dayton Accords and the constitution define as entities. I have to emphasise that the agreement and the constitution avoid, presumably very precisely, to use the term "state" when referring to the entities. What, at first glance, looks like a constitutional argument, a dispute about the constitutional organisation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is in point of fact a purely political argument, but that is not something that is of much interest to the Judges. And the governments of the federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the Republika Srpska are institutions with identical powers, but they do not operate in the same way, because the internal order, the internal organisation, of these two entities is different. Republika Srpska belongs to a type of unitarian state, centralised, and the federation, as its name shows, is a composite state. The constituent elements of which are, in terms of the law of state, of state law, are counties, that is, cantons much which there are ten whose terms of reference are such that they can have their autonomous governments and autonomous representative bodies. Another uncommon [Realtime transcript read in error "and common"] thing concerning the government of the federation, which stems from the climate of mutual distrust. Here this is not "common" but "uncommon". So another uncommon aspect of the government of the federation is that it has ministers and deputy ministers with almost identical rights. The offices are distributed on the parity basis between the Croats and Muslims, that is, Bosniaks, and a minister and his deputy cannot come from the same people. At the same time, no act becomes final and valid unless it has been co-signed by the relevant minister and his deputy. And that would be it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, expert. I've been waiting for somebody to explain it for a full year. What is the reality of Bosnia and Herzegovina and now I wish to -- I want to ask you -- I received a letter from the minister of defence of the federation in which he says that the he would be very happy to allow me access to the archive but that his deputy minister does not allow it and that is what you just --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: That is the reality. A minister cannot meet your request unless it is also approved by his deputy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I have given this document to be translated because on the basis of this, I will also seek -- but that doesn't matter. I wanted to hear your explanation. We are moving towards the end. Two questions which have also been preoccupying us here: Are you aware of any ultimatum of April 1993 that would issued by the HZ HB to the Muslims, Bosniaks?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. I am aware of this ultimatum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it really an ultimatum or is it something else? I want an explanation.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I am aware of the ultimatum from the expert opinion of Dr. Donia's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Can you?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: What struck me as odd was that Dr. Donia relied on two newspaper comments referring to this ultimatum in his expert opinion. This ultimatum, as interpreted, and it needs to be interpreted within the whole context of the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, in my judgement, is a kind of political pressure, it at the same -- on a par with, say, the decision of the constitutional court of 1992 on the unlawfulness, illegality of the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Interesting. Now, my one-before-the-last question. As a historian, have you had an opportunity to come across or see the transcripts, alleged, in inverted commas, or authentic ones, from President Tudjman's office? And if yes, tell us what it is about. And how do you see them? What do you think of them?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I have come across this material in a book by Ciril Rebicic, who was another expert in this honourable court.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On whose side?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor's. In his book, published in Zagreb, published the transcript of an audio recording, from a meeting which Dr. Franjo Tudjman held with representatives of the HDZ from Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the meeting on the 27th of December, 1991?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes. That is the record or rather the transcript because minutes is a much stricter defined term than what we are dealing with here. Moreover, in different papers in Croatia --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Different papers?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: [In English] Newspapers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: See how it's translated?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about newspapers, about the press, written press. So in these newspapers, texts were published and a claim was made that they represented transcripts of the audio recordings done during meetings which President Tudjman held in his residence. The problem regarding these texts, and I deliberately say "texts," is very simple for a professional historian. There is no guarantee that these are authentic documents. The audio recording itself is missing. Those papers have no official authentication. And a historian must, in the first place, establish to what extent is a document what it purports to be. In this case, it is impossible to establish. Namely, although these texts circulate, the originals are not accessible. So that it is impossible to establish whether they are truly what they presume to be. On the other hand, what I read in Ciril Ribicic's book, namely what is printed there as a conversation, as a record of a conversation, as a historian, I cannot really fully judge it because I do not have an insight into what previous conversations, preceding conversations, looked like, all the people that President Tudjman met, what kind of information he had at his disposal, and how those conversations were interpreted later on in subsequent conversations, and these are all the elements which must underpin the evaluation of such material. What can be done on the basis of a text edited in this manner is to discern a situation in which a man who maintains permanent contact with representatives of what we call today the international community, it is a man who is aware, who realises that the decision on the future of Bosnia-Herzegovina is taken by and large by representatives of that international community, and that this is indeed so, that it has indeed been so during the past few hundred years is attested to by Misha Glenny's books, Stavrianos, an American historian of Greek origin and so on and so forth. I won't now list them all. In their books, they all show how, in, on the Balkan peninsula, relevant political decisions have always been made by representatives of the big powers. In contrast, therefore, with a man who realises that, and across the man who realises it, there sit people who come from their small milieus, who believe in their messianic role and who believe that they have a prescription for the solution to the crisis in Bosnia and Herzegovina. The atmosphere at that meeting, and I can speak only about my impressions about the atmosphere, if the things which are written there are true, that atmosphere therefore is as follows: An attempt by that man to people gathered there, to confirm their importance to the people gathered there, to, on the other hand, hear what they think. And thirdly to try to transmit to them that most important message, that in spite of their wishes, they will not be the ones who will decide on the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I left this question for the very end, because again, for a year, I've been listening to something in this courtroom. I've been listening to references played to the Banovina of Croatia. Mr. Usher, you can use my copy. I know this by heart anyway. This is Exhibit P899. Oh, yes, oh, yes. In my opinion, until now, nobody explained the time, circumstances, what happened, and how come this happened, and where this name came from. Nobody explained this to the Trial Chamber. I've been listening to this for a year now, that President Tudjman wanted to establish the banovina to the detriment of Bosnia-Herzegovina. I would like to hear your expert's opinion. That is my last question. That is exactly the amount of time that we have left until the break. So that you can explain the time circumstances, the historical circumstances, and everything else to the Trial Chamber, and could you please explain whether this has anything to do with 1992.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It would be pretentious on my part to believe that I can explain what Dr. Tudjman actually meant, and I hope that that is not what you're asking me to do, because after all, after 50 years' time, perhaps some papers will surface that will shed new light on all these problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: By all means. I meant that you should explain these historical circumstances using this map because that is what has been shown here time and again.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I have understood that perfectly, but I have to say what I cannot do. What is called banovina --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You can also use your pointer and show this on the map.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Banovina is an attempt made in 1939 to resolve the problems in the relations between the Serbs and Croats, but please, this was 1939. That was a time, and actually now we are going back to what we debated, so to speak, during the first part. At that time, nobody took Bosnia-Herzegovina seriously as a separate problem or the Muslim population in Bosnia-Herzegovina as a serious problem. And as a historian, I have to warn about that. There are very different circumstances involved in terms of when something happens. So to transfer a situation from 1992 into 1939 is the same kind of nonsensical thing like transferring the situation of 1939 to 1992. Another question that is important to explain what the banovina is, the Banovina of Croatia, that's what it was called, was created by observing the borders, the administrative borders, of a body which, until 1918, was called the Kingdom of Croatia, Dalmatia and Slavonia, and to this territory was added a territory which at that point in time, the Croat population outnumbered the Serb population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me. In that year, in 1939, was there a Muslim or a Bosniak nation?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: There were certainly ideas about that in certain circles, ideas that this is a separate community, but this is not a subject of public discourse. In political relations, no one was thinking in those terms, because a distinction has to be made here as to what political reality is and what future potential is. And that point in time, there were certainly foundations out of which a new nation would grow, but that is not a reality in political life yet. In 1939, no one could think in terms of what was topical in 1971 or 1972.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please look at this pink-coloured thing here within the banovina. What was it called in 1939, the pink thing in the middle, in the middle of the banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, what was it that called?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: At that time that was called the Savska Banovina. I'm sorry, not Savska banovina, the Vrbaska Banovina. The green area up here is Savska Banovina. And all of then Yugoslavia was divided into banovinas. So the Banovina of Croatia was not an exception in terms of the setup existing throughout the former Yugoslavia then. It is not even an exception in terms of the fact that its majority population were Croats, because Savska banovina at that time was populated by Slovenians only. So that would be it. That would be the historical context of the banovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Expert, sir, that was my last question. I thank you for having come and for having helped all of us with your testimony to understand certain things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have concluded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, it's time for a break, I think. We will resume at ten minutes past 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Cross-examination. Mr. Scott? Cross-examined by Mr. Scott:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, sir.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get too far away from it, sir, I want to ask you a couple of questions. Toward the end of your direct testimony in connection with the ultimatum in April, 1993, you said that this was a kind of political pressure. Can you please explain a bit more about, first of all, political pressure by who? Who was exercising this political pressure?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Well, obviously, at that point in time, it was exercised by the HVO against the other side in the conflict, which had not yet attained the form of an open conflict. As far as it can be discerned today, the pressure had a very definite objective. The objective was to try to win over the then-still-Muslim side to accept fully the provisions of the Vance-Owen Plan.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would it be more accurate to say, sir, I don't question what you've said but at all, in fact, but would it be more accurate to say that it was pressure on the Muslim side to accept the HVO vision of the Vance-Owen Plan?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Perhaps it would be quite accurate but we would have to take into account the fact that Vance and Owen had one vision of the plan and they were the ones who conceived of it, and then another vision was on the side of the Croats, and a third on the side of the Muslims, and fourth the representatives, the political representatives of the Serbs and so on and so forth so then we could speak about a countless number of visions of this agreement.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now n your report, you say that the rise of Serbian nationalism, I'm referring to page 22 of the English version, or the translation, the rise of Serbian nationalism calls the same reaction everywhere, that is the awakening or awaking and rise of another nationalisms. Do I understand correctly, sir, when you say "other nationalisms" you include in that nationalisms to use that phrase, if I can say it that way, nationalisms of the Muslim group, and nationalisms among the Croats?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: If we wish to be quite accurate, then we would proceed from the following: That every form of national determination is situation-bound. In any situation, when a given group accentuates its own national identity, this inevitably causes a reaction on the part of those who do not belong to that group. I was speaking in that sense, not only about the Croats, about the Muslims too. But also about the Slovenians, the Macedonians, the Albanians, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. I appreciate that, sir. I just wanted to make sure that you were not limiting that comment or your conclusion or observation in that regard to only the Serbs but that you found that to be true about the Muslims and Croats as well. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: I don't really understand what is the same as in the case of the Serbs. I don't really understand your question because obviously it cannot be the same.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, you said the same reaction, that the rise of Serbian nationalism caused the same reaction everywhere, the awakening and rise of other nationalisms and my earlier question to you, and I thought we were essentially in agreement on, was that when you say "other nationalisms" you include in that Muslim nationalism and Croat nationalism.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Generally speaking, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And at page 16 of your report, sir, you say this: "That constant conflicts over disputed territories inhabited by," in your paper "minorities" and "diasporas" permanently seeking a way to join the "mother national state" can you explain to the Judges in that context what you mean by the phrase "mother national state"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: A "mother national state" is something which, in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, exists only in the case of the Serbs. National states then, according to that logic, the mother state or this kind of perception, does not exist in any other case, because before 1991, there were no other nation-states. However, it is possible to speak about territories, about where this is generated, and in which way. That is to say this feeling of belonging to a particular community. And then how that feeling is manifested.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
