utterances.text: It's true, is it not, sir, that your statement about mother national states after the recognition of Croatia as an independent country, would also apply to Croatia, wouldn't it? That was another mother national state in relation to one of the main ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina, correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The problem that you are raising here implies a very complex answer. What you are implying in your question is something that I would not accept, because the process of Yugoslavia's disintegration is a very complex set of events in which, from the point of view of day to day events, and that is definitely the perception that the participants had, things are viewed in a special way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, on page 23 of your report, filed with the judges, do you not say "another important fact became clearly visible. Two of the three local nations did not link their future to Bosnia-Herzegovina but to their again 'mother countries,'" in reference to the Croats and Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. Their political loyalty was linked to the notions of Croatia and Serbia. According to the logic of the fact that they are Croats and Serbs respectively.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how did this manifest itself, this linkage to the two mother countries, respectively, Croatia and Serbia? What did you see as a historian that supports the statement at page 23 of your report?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: What I meant when I wrote what I wrote on page 23 was the fact that could be discerned from the public discourse. That is, that these people would like to live within the same state frameworks respectively with the other members of their ethnic community.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say public discourse, I take it you would include political discourse in that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. To the extent to which such things were discussed by people at lower levels of the political establishment. In my opinion, it is very significant that the top echelons of the political establishment never talked about it in such a way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll come to that eventually, I'm sure. But you agree, in fact again on page 23, and for those who may be following just a few lines below the passage I directed your attention to a few moment ago, sir, you agree in your paper that the HDZ party in Bosnia and Herzegovina was a local branch of Franjo Tudjman's HDZ party established in Croatia, correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: As usual, every sentence has its own context. If you mean by way of a context that the HDZ of the B and H was established and started to operate at the moment while Yugoslavia was still in existence, and which is very important to note, then that is a quotation that is correct. However, at any rate, along with such a quotation, one should always highlight the context as well. At that point in time, no one thought that political organisations are to be confined to the borders of the then socialist republics. The pattern for organising political parties was the existing League of Communists, which was actually a political organisation throughout the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, at this point in time, I'm just simply trying to make sure that I understand some of the basic points in your paper. I don't believe it's fair to say that I've taken anything out of context. I refer you again to page 23 much your report. And to read to you exactly I will quote the English language of the two points that I've just asked you about. Your report says, "Another important fact became clearly visible. Two of the three local nations did not link their future to Bosnia-Herzegovina but to their mother countries. Both Croats and Serbs, primed by events in Yugoslavia since the late 1980s and their firm networks of primary social [family] links with Croatia and Serbia, turned out en masse for the local branches of parties previously established in Croatia, the Croats for the HDZ, the Serbs for the SDS." Now, I've read that correctly, haven't I?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And following on from that, at page 26 of your report, you said that "the strength and attraction of the party lay in the fact" -- in reference to the HDZ -- "the strength and attraction of the party lay in the fact that at that time, it had already come to power in neighbouring Croatia and that the Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina therefore saw it as a 'Croatian party' with its seat in Zagreb." Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. That is what it says in my text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you go on to say that the voters, the Bosnian Croat voters, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, saw as the real leader of the HDZ both in Croatia and Bosnia-Herzegovina, as Franjo Tudjman. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I say in the text.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, one of the -- I'm going to ask you for several more is the reason I'm going to ask you this but just so you know where I'm coming from and where I'm going. One of the items that you give in support of your position, your assessment of the role of Franjo Tudjman was his role concerning a JNA convoy going through a certain part of Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1991. And you said at page 27, "This was a clear indicator of who enjoyed real authority and whose word had actual political weight." And again, I understand, sir, that you base that in part on this anecdote about the convoy.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: May I just have a minute or two so that I could find my text in the Croatian language so that I can check exactly what it says there?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: Mr. Scott, can I say something? Your form of cross-examination of this expert and the last expert are a little unfair, are they not? You're very familiar with the little excerpts that you're going to quote from and just to throw them in rapid succession at the expert, I don't think that serves any real purpose. Why don't you put your thesis to him and then say, "Didn't you say something else?" Because you've gone sort of through about six or eight different excerpts very, very rapidly and unless Professor Ancic knows his report by heart it's very difficult for him. Perhaps we have to be a little more fair. An expert isn't a machine.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Judge Clark, he can take as much time -- it is his report, after all, he wrote it, and as was in my respectful submission, I choose my words carefully, a matter of some concern with the previous witness, is that sometimes what appear to be said on the face of his report was not in fact apparently what he meant at all. And that's why I want to confirm that I, in fact, do understand what's being said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I think I know which expert report you're talking about and I think that we all agreed that there were problems with some -- I'm being careful with my words, too -- a translation that wasn't of the standard that we are used to, shall I say that? Which made it very, very difficult for us to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CLARK
utterances.text: I don't think that's the problem here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Well, let me build upon the last question, if you found that place in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Scott, I think the witness would like to say something.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Your Honours, what perplexed me was the interpretation I got just now, the interpretation of the Prosecutor's question, namely in my text, I refer to "authority" in the sense of political authority, and the interpretation I got meant authorities in the sense of government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I appreciate that, sir. All I can do obviously is read as accurately as I possibly can from the English translation of your report. And unfortunately how that comes to your ears I can't control that. But I appreciate the clarification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krsnik?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We have come to a certain point and I thank the Honourable Judge Clark for her intervention I had meant to do this too but now it's pointless of course because the Prosecutor said "authority" in English and it was translated into the Croatian language properly, "authority" but that is not what the Croatian text says. In his cross-examination, the Prosecutor resorted to tricks. Perhaps I should put it that way. And that is obvious from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I believe that the Prosecutor just reads what was said on the page 27 of that report. I don't see any differences. Maybe, Mr. Scott, you may read that paragraph once again so that we could know which paragraph we are talking about, at least I found that exceptions in page 27.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: The top of page 27, sir, and all I can do, sir, I regret, is to read from the English translation I have been provided of your report. And I can read -- I read it this way, and if I misread it I'm sure someone in the courtroom will correct me. "The situation changed, however, when the assembled mass was addressed directly via television by Dr. Tudjman, after his assurances, the crowd dispersed and the military column went on its way. Even for those who were completely uninformed, this was a very clear indicator of who enjoyed real authority and whose word had actual political weight." Now, I think at this point the only question -- did I read it correctly?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes. It was correctly read, probably, and this time it was properly interpreted into the Croatian language. I certainly hope that the honourable Trial Chamber notes the distinction between "authority" on the one hand, and the authorities on the other hand. Political authority is a matter of conviction, and authorities is supervision over the mechanisms of the state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And during the time, sir, from at least 1991 to 1995, there was no single person in the Republic of Croatia who more made and represented Croatian state policy than Franjo Tudjman, correct?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It is. His constitutional duty was to conduct the state policy and that is why he won the confidence of the voters in the elections, and that was his duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you also say in your report, sir, and is it correct, is it your observation, or assessment, that the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina was a war for territory?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Or.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Or - and that would be much more accurate - that it turned into a war for territories, that the dynamics of the conflict, which began in 1992 as one form of the conflict, led to -- resulted in the fact that it changed its nature and goals set by those who waged it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say at pages 23 and 24 of your report that the Serb nationalist movement had a developed strategy of how to present its attempts in the media and hide its true aims and methods. What do you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: As regards what you have just said, I found confirmation of it in a debate already mentioned between political scientists -- by political scientist Danielle Conversini. What I meant by this is the fact that the attempt to separate a part of Yugoslavia was publicly presented as an attempt to preserve Yugoslavia, as a well-organised system, the political establishment in Belgrade also had an elaborate strategy of their media presentations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the strategy, sir? And what were some of the ways it was carried out?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Well, the strategy was as I have just said. Not to allow the real goals, which undoubtedly could not count with the support by relevant parts of the international community, to disguise and therefore they were disguised by acceptable explanations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, you say, about the beginning of the mutual conflict between the Croats and the Bosniaks or Muslims, and this is covered on page 25 of your report, you said that, unlike the Serbian nationalists who were evidently working from a plan drawn up and developed in advance, the Croats and Bosniaks or Muslims were clearly acting chaotically and with a high level of disorganization until the time of their mutual conflict. My first question about that, sir, was when do you mark, because there has been much discussion, as Mr. Krsnik says, in the past year, when do you mark as the beginning of the time of their mutual conflict?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: The beginning of the conflict could be placed tentatively in the latter half of May, but, although by that time it was already clear that the views about the political future of Bosnia and Herzegovina diverged significantly and that they could result in a general conflict, that conflict did not yet acquire the dimensions of a general one until well into -- until July, 1992. On the other hand, different forms of conflict emerged from different contexts, could be observed as of the beginning of 1992. The first conflict that can be considered a real conflict is the one which broke out in Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when was that, sir, for the record and for the Judges? What conflict are you talking about in Busovaca and the date, please?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: It was in May, 1992, at a moment when, from the barracks in Busovaca, when the Yugoslav People's Army withdrew from the barracks in Busovaca. The conflict broke out when the troops left the barracks and when Muslim, Muslims still at that time, Bosniak, soldiers, entered the barracks and tried to change the already-existing understanding about the distribution of weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, before we get --

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: Namely --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I apologise for interrupting you but before we lose it on the screen and get too far away, at the beginning of your answer just now, you said, actually now it's your prior answer you said, "The beginning of the conflict could be placed tentatively in the latter half of May." At that point in time, sir, you didn't give us a year. Could you give us which year you were talking about there?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Krsnik, what's the problem?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRSNIK
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the problem is that the witness must be allowed to, that the Prosecutor interrupted him through mid-sentence and halfway through his thought, and he can resume his interrogation after the witness is allowed to finish his sentence and his thought. How shall we understand what happened in Busovaca if the witness was interrupted halfway through his thought? And the Prosecutor can take him back where he wants to after we have heard the whole answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, the translation, as you know, the translation stopped, I took it that was the end of the answer and that's exactly when I did try to go back. Then the witness started speaking again. So that's all that was -- that's all that need be said, I believe, about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I think that is a misunderstanding. Witness, would you please furnish us with the years first? And then the Prosecutor will go on for your question. And if you did not finish your answer, you're allowed to continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, let me go back to where I started. I think I said that the conflict started in May, what we might call the general conflict. That had its beginning in May, 1993. Individual conflicts, however, lasted -- and that is what I was referring to, that example -- have been lasting since May, 1992, and if I am -- I may be allowed to finish, I'd be happy to finish my tale about what caused the first such conflict that I know about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I never stopped you sir. All I did was try to get the date which you finally did give us when Judge Liu asked you. So that was my only question. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: So the conflict in Busovaca broke out after the Muslim side, the Bosniak side, having been the first to enter the barracks premises, tried to change the already-existing agreement on the distribution of weapons. And the reasoning behind it was that the Croats had more weapons anyway. And in that situation, the Muslim side demanded, on the basis of its advantage of having the first to be -- to enter the barracks, the majority of the weapons there. At that time I lived in Sarajevo and about that conflict I heard the reports on the radio. Fortunately, I was in a situation to even see it on television. And also to read the written report in the Oslobodjenje daily. So what I just told you is the version that I learned in Sarajevo. Such conflicts, individual, were occurring for the whole year between May, 1992 and May, 1993. They broke out within different contexts, but they generated an atmosphere of mutual distrust and thus provided conditions in which local conflicts could then grow into an all-out conflict. That is what I wanted to say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that by mid-1992, in this regard, in the context that you've just given us, that by mid-1992, ethnic nationalism had become, in your terms, "the only real value and beacon for the population." Page 27 of your report. Can you explain to us a bit further what you mean when you say -- when you say that by mid-1992, "ethnic nationalism had become the only real value"?

utterances.speaker: MLADEN ANCIC
utterances.text: What I wanted to say is in the previous sentence, the sentence preceding that one, and I will read it out in Croatian. I hope you have it translated into English. "In a situation in which there was no longer an organised state apparatus of coercion, without the moral and political authority to support former solidarity networks at the microsocial level, and with a deeply rooted experience of life in silent, latent segregation, the ethnic nationalism did not become, it remained, it was left as the only real shelter of collective consciousness." If you want a more detailed explanation of the notions what it means, the solidarity or solidarious [phoen] networks or silent segregation, in inverted commas, because these terms have a special definition, then, of course, I could spend at it a great deal of time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
